Romans 1.summary: Paul introduces himself as an apostle entrusted with the gospel about Jesus Christ, descended from David and declared Son of God in power through resurrection (Romans 1:1–7). He thanks God for Rome's believers and hopes to visit them (Romans 1:8–15). The gospel reveals God's righteousness and offers salvation to everyone who believes, Jew and Greek alike (Romans 1:16–17). Paul then describes humanity's suppression of the truth, exchange of worship of the Creator for created things, and the ensuing pattern of distorted desires and destructive behavior (Romans 1:18–32). The chapter establishes both the good news and the serious problem of human rebellion that Paul's argument will address.
Romans 1.whereWeAre: Acts closed with Paul under guard in Rome, preaching the kingdom of God to all who came to him (Acts 28:30-31). Romans is the letter he wrote to that city's believers before ever reaching it: he introduces himself as an apostle, says he longs to visit them, and states his theme that the gospel is God's power to save everyone who believes, before describing why the whole world needs it (1:1-32). That diagnosis of human sin turns in chapter 2 toward the person who judges others.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Introduces himself as an apostle set apart for the gospel, thanks God for Rome's faith, and says he has long wanted to visit them (1:1-15).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: The subject of the gospel, descended from David and declared the Son of God with power by the resurrection from the dead (1:3-4).

keyFigures.name: Believers in Rome
keyFigures.role: Addressed as beloved of God and called to be saints, with a faith spoken of throughout the whole world (1:7-8).

keyFigures.name: Gentiles and Greeks
keyFigures.role: Named with the Jews as those the gospel is for, and as those who suppressed the truth about God and turned to idols (1:14,16,18-25).

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Reveals his righteousness in the gospel and his wrath against ungodliness, and gives people up to what they have chosen (1:17-18,24-28).

keyThemes.explanation: Paul says the gospel is the power of God unto salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek (1:16-17).
Though God's power is plain in creation, people changed the truth of God into a lie and worshiped the creature more than the Creator (1:18-25).
Paul lists the evils that follow when God gives people up to what they chose, and says those who do them are without excuse (1:28-32).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the declaration that the righteous shall live by faith.

Romans 2.summary: Paul turns the accusation toward those who judge others while doing comparable wrongs (Romans 2:1–5). God's judgment is impartial and considers deeds rather than reputation (Romans 2:6–11). Paul considers people with and without the written Law, including conscience and accountability (Romans 2:12–16). He then addresses a person who identifies as Jewish, values the Law, and yet may fail to practice its requirements (Romans 2:17–24). Circumcision is meaningful when paired with obedience; Paul contrasts outward identity with an inward orientation of the heart (Romans 2:25–29). His central challenge is that possession of sacred instruction does not by itself establish righteousness.
Romans 2.whereWeAre: Chapter 1 ended with Paul describing a world that exchanged the truth about God for idols (1:18-32). Chapter 2 turns on the reader who agrees and feels superior: God judges everyone impartially by their deeds, those with the written law and those without it, and having the law or circumcision is not enough without a changed heart (2:1-29). That levels the ground for chapter 3's question about what advantage the Jew has.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Confronts judging and complacency by speaking directly to an imagined questioner and to one who calls himself a Jew (2:1,17).

keyFigures.name: The judging person
keyFigures.role: A representative objector who condemns others while doing the same things, and is told God's goodness is meant to lead him to repentance (2:1-5).

keyFigures.name: Jews and Gentiles
keyFigures.role: Both are judged by deeds without partiality, whether they have the written law or only a conscience that bears witness (2:9-16).

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Judges each person impartially according to deeds and sees the secrets of the heart through Jesus Christ (2:6,11,16).

keyThemes.explanation: God will render to every man according to his deeds, for there is no respect of persons with God (2:6-11).
Not the hearers of the law but the doers are justified, and even Gentiles show the law written in their hearts through conscience (2:12-16).
Circumcision matters only with obedience, and a true Jew is one inwardly, whose circumcision is of the heart (2:25-29).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the declaration that God's name is blasphemed among the Gentiles.

Romans 3.summary: Paul asks whether Jewish identity and circumcision have any advantage and answers that Jews were entrusted with God's oracles (Romans 3:1–2). Human unfaithfulness does not nullify God's faithfulness (Romans 3:3–8). He then gathers scriptural quotations to portray the universality of sin (Romans 3:9–20). The decisive shift comes when Paul says God's righteousness has been disclosed apart from the Law, though witnessed by the Law and Prophets: justification is through faith in Jesus Christ for believers, with no distinction, because all have sinned (Romans 3:21–26). Boasting is excluded; God is God of Jews and Gentiles, and faith does not cancel the Law (Romans 3:27–31). This is a central presentation of Paul's account of divine grace and human need.
Romans 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with Paul saying true circumcision is of the heart, not the flesh (2:28-29). Chapter 3 asks what advantage the Jew has, answers that Israel was entrusted with God's words, then strings together Scripture to show that Jews and Gentiles are alike under sin before announcing that God's righteousness comes through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe (3:1-31). Chapter 4 tests that claim against Abraham.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Answers what advantage the Jew has, gathers Scripture to show all are under sin, and explains righteousness through faith (3:1-31).

keyFigures.name: Jews and Gentiles
keyFigures.role: Shown by a chain of Psalms and Isaiah to be alike under sin, and both justified by faith in the one God (3:9-20,29-30).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Set forth by God as a propitiation through faith in his blood, the redemption by which believers are justified freely (3:24-25).

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Stays faithful though every man is a liar, and is both just and the justifier of the one who believes in Jesus (3:3-4,26).

keyThemes.explanation: A chain of Psalms and Isaiah shows that there is none righteous, no, not one, and every mouth is stopped before God (3:9-20).
All have sinned, and believers are justified freely by God's grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus (3:21-26).
Boasting is excluded, since the one God justifies both the circumcised and the uncircumcised by faith (3:27-31).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the words about God being justified in his sayings.
Paul cites the psalm's statement that none does good and none seeks God.
Paul quotes the psalm's declaration that no one does good or seeks God.
Paul quotes the description of poison beneath deceitful lips.
Paul quotes the description of an open grave as an image of deceitful speech.
Paul quotes the description of a mouth full of cursing and bitterness.
Paul quotes Isaiah's words about feet swift to shed blood and not knowing peace.
Paul quotes the declaration that there is no fear of God before their eyes.

Romans 4.summary: Paul uses Abraham as the main scriptural example for his teaching on faith. Genesis says Abraham believed God and it was credited to him as righteousness before his circumcision (Romans 4:1–12). David is quoted on the blessing of forgiven sins (Romans 4:6–8). Abraham's promise was not based on law-keeping but on faith; therefore he can be portrayed as father of both circumcised and uncircumcised believers (Romans 4:13–17). Although Abraham faced physical limits and circumstances that made the promise seem impossible, he trusted God's capacity to give life (Romans 4:18–22). Paul then connects the statement about righteousness being credited to Abraham to those who believe in God who raised Jesus (Romans 4:23–25).
Romans 4.whereWeAre: Chapter 3 ended with Paul saying that faith does not cancel the law but establishes it (3:31). Chapter 4 proves the point from Scripture: Abraham believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness before he was circumcised, and David describes the same blessing of forgiven sin (4:1-25). That faith, resting on God who raises the dead, opens chapter 5's picture of peace with God.

keyFigures.name: Abraham
keyFigures.role: Believed God and it was counted to him for righteousness before he was circumcised, making him father of all who believe (4:3,9-12).

keyFigures.name: David
keyFigures.role: Quoted by Paul as describing the blessing of the person whose sins are forgiven and not counted against him (4:6-8).

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Reads Genesis and the Psalms to show that righteousness comes by faith, not works, and applies it to those who believe in God who raised Jesus (4:1-25).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Delivered for our offences and raised again for our justification (4:24-25).

keyThemes.explanation: Abraham was counted righteous in Genesis 15, before he was circumcised in Genesis 17, so he is father of all who believe (4:9-12).
The promise came through the righteousness of faith, not the law, so that it might be by grace and sure to all the seed (4:13-17).
Abraham, nearly a hundred years old, did not stagger at the promise but was fully persuaded that God could perform it (4:18-25).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes Abraham believing God and it being counted as righteousness.
Paul quotes David's words about forgiven sin.
Paul quotes God's declaration making Abraham father of many nations.
Paul quotes the promise that Abraham's descendants would be numerous.

Romans 5.summary: Having argued for justification through faith, Paul describes peace with God, access to grace, hope, and the possibility of endurance amid suffering (Romans 5:1–5). He emphasizes that Christ died for sinners and enemies as an expression of divine love and reconciliation (Romans 5:6–11). Paul then contrasts Adam and Christ: sin and death entered through one man, while the grace and life offered through Christ surpass the consequences of Adam's disobedience (Romans 5:12–21). The chapter moves from the believer's present relationship with God to a sweeping account of humanity's plight and grace's abundance. Christians disagree over some particulars of how Adam's sin affects descendants, but Paul clearly contrasts sin's reign with grace.
Romans 5.whereWeAre: Chapter 4 ended with Jesus delivered for our offences and raised for our justification (4:25). Chapter 5 describes what that gives believers, peace with God and hope in suffering, then widens to compare Adam, through whom sin and death entered the world, with Christ, through whom grace and life abound (5:1-21). Grace's abundance raises the question chapter 6 answers.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Moves from peace with God through justification to a comparison of Adam and Christ (5:1-21).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Dies for the ungodly while they are still sinners, and through his one act of obedience brings justification of life to many (5:6-8,18-19).

keyFigures.name: Adam
keyFigures.role: The one man through whom sin entered the world, and death by sin, passing to all (5:12-14).

keyFigures.name: Believers
keyFigures.role: Have peace with God, access into grace, and a hope that does not shame them, even in tribulation (5:1-5).

keyThemes.explanation: Justified by faith, believers have peace with God, access into grace, and a hope that does not make ashamed even in tribulation (5:1-5).
God commended his love in that Christ died for us while we were yet sinners, and we were reconciled while enemies (5:6-11).
Sin and death entered through one man, but the gift of grace by one man, Jesus Christ, abounds much more (5:12-21).

Romans 6.summary: Paul rejects the idea that grace encourages continued wrongdoing (Romans 6:1–2). Baptism into Christ is described as participation in his death and resurrection, symbolizing death to sin and newness of life (Romans 6:3–11). Believers should therefore not let sin rule their bodies but offer themselves to God (Romans 6:12–14). Through an analogy of service, Paul contrasts slavery to sin, which leads to death, with obedience that leads toward righteousness and holiness (Romans 6:15–23). He concludes that sin pays wages of death, while eternal life is God's gift in Christ (Romans 6:23). The chapter makes a practical case that grace calls for transformed living.
Romans 6.whereWeAre: Chapter 5 ended with grace abounding where sin abounded (5:20-21). Chapter 6 answers the objection that this invites more sinning: believers were baptized into Christ's death and resurrection, so they are to count themselves dead to sin, offer themselves to God, and serve righteousness instead of sin (6:1-23). Chapter 7 turns to the law's place in that freedom.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Rejects the idea that believers should keep sinning so grace can abound, using baptism and slavery as his pictures (6:1-23).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Died and was raised, so that those baptized into him walk in newness of life (6:3-10).

keyFigures.name: Baptized believers
keyFigures.role: Told to count themselves dead to sin and alive to God, and to yield their members to him as instruments of righteousness (6:11-13).

keyThemes.explanation: Buried with Christ by baptism into death, believers are raised to walk in newness of life (6:3-11).

keyThemes.theme: Grace is not permission to sin
keyThemes.explanation: Paul answers the question whether to continue in sin that grace may abound with God forbid, since believers died to sin (6:1-2).
Everyone serves something, sin that pays death or obedience that leads to righteousness, and eternal life is God's gift through Jesus Christ (6:15-23).

Romans 7.summary: Paul first uses marriage as an analogy for how death changes a legal relationship, explaining that believers have died to the Law through Christ in order to bear fruit for God (Romans 7:1–6). He insists that the Law itself is not sin: the commandment exposes sin, which misuses what is good (Romans 7:7–13). Then a dramatic first-person passage describes the struggle of willing the good yet doing what is hated, and the conflict between delight in God's Law and a force of sin at work (Romans 7:14–24). The chapter ends with thanksgiving to God through Jesus Christ (Romans 7:25). Readers have understood the first-person voice as Paul’s own present experience, his life before Christ, Israel, or a representative human being; the passage emphasizes sin's power and the Law's inability by itself to liberate.
Romans 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 ended with the wages of sin set against God's gift of eternal life (6:23). Chapter 7 uses marriage to explain how believers have died to the law, defends the law as holy and good, and describes in the first person the struggle of knowing the good yet doing what is hated, ending in thanks to God through Jesus Christ (7:1-25). That cry for deliverance is answered in chapter 8.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Uses marriage law to show believers have died to the law through Christ, then defends the law as holy and just (7:1-13).

keyFigures.name: The first-person “I”
keyFigures.role: The voice of 7:7-25, who delights in God's law yet finds another law at work in his members and cries out for deliverance (7:7-24).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Named in the closing thanksgiving as the one through whom God delivers from the body of this death (7:24-25).

keyThemes.explanation: The law is holy, just, and good; it is sin that took occasion by the commandment and worked death (7:7-13).
Paul describes willing the good but doing the evil he hates, a war between the law of his mind and the law in his members (7:14-24).
The cry, who shall deliver me from the body of this death, is answered with thanks to God through Jesus Christ our Lord (7:24-25).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the commandment not to covet.

Romans 8.summary: Paul proclaims no condemnation for those in Christ and describes liberation by the Spirit from sin and death (Romans 8:1–11). Believers are called to live by the Spirit, not the flesh, and are named God's children and heirs who can address God as Father (Romans 8:12–17). Present suffering is set against future glory; creation groans, believers await bodily redemption, and the Spirit helps them in weakness (Romans 8:18–27). Paul affirms God's purpose for those called and asks a series of questions about accusation, condemnation, suffering, and separation (Romans 8:28–39). The chapter climaxes by declaring that nothing in all creation can separate believers from God's love in Christ. The 'flesh' and 'Spirit' contrast concerns competing orientations of life, not a simple rejection of the physical body.
Romans 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 ended with Paul thanking God through Jesus Christ for deliverance from the body of this death (7:24-25). Chapter 8 declares no condemnation for those in Christ, describes life by the Spirit, adoption as God's children, and creation groaning for redemption, and closes with the assurance that nothing can separate believers from God's love (8:1-39). Chapter 9 turns to Paul's sorrow over his own people.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Declares no condemnation for those in Christ and ends with a list of things that cannot separate believers from God's love (8:1,35-39).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Died, rose, and makes intercession at the right hand of God, so that nothing can separate believers from his love (8:34-35).

keyFigures.name: Holy Spirit
keyFigures.role: Frees believers from the law of sin and death, bears witness that they are children of God, and helps their weakness with groanings that cannot be uttered (8:2,15-16,26).

keyFigures.name: Believers and creation
keyFigures.role: Both groan while waiting for redemption, believers as adopted children and the creation as in the pains of childbirth (8:19-23).

keyThemes.explanation: There is no condemnation to those in Christ Jesus, because the law of the Spirit of life has made them free from the law of sin and death (8:1-11).
Those led by the Spirit are children and heirs of God, and present sufferings are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory (8:12-25).
If God is for us, nothing, not death, life, nor any other creature, can separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus (8:31-39).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the psalm about being counted as sheep for slaughter.

Romans 9.summary: Paul begins with profound grief for fellow Israelites and lists Israel's covenant privileges (Romans 9:1–5). He argues that God's promise has not failed, distinguishing descent from participation in the promise through examples involving Isaac, Ishmael, Jacob, and Esau (Romans 9:6–13). He then asks whether God is unjust and invokes Moses, Pharaoh, and the potter-clay image to discuss divine mercy and freedom (Romans 9:14–24). Quotations from Hosea and Isaiah frame God's calling of Gentiles and the preservation of a remnant of Israel (Romans 9:25–29). Paul concludes by contrasting Gentiles receiving righteousness by faith with Israel's pursuit through works understood as a stumbling over Christ (Romans 9:30–33). Interpretations of election and human freedom differ widely; the chapter belongs to Paul's larger discussion of Israel in chapters 9–11.
Romans 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 ended with nothing able to separate believers from the love of God (8:38-39). Chapter 9 raises the painful question that assurance invites, whether God's word to Israel has failed: Paul grieves for his kinsmen, shows that the promise follows God's call through Isaac and Jacob, and describes God's mercy toward Jews and Gentiles alike (9:1-33). Chapter 10 continues with Israel's response.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Grieves over his kinsmen according to the flesh and argues that God's word to Israel has not failed (9:1-6).

keyFigures.name: Israelites
keyFigures.role: Paul's kinsmen, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, and the promises (9:3-5).

keyFigures.name: Isaac, Ishmael, Jacob and Esau
keyFigures.role: Genesis figures through whom Paul shows that the promise follows God's call, not physical descent alone (9:7-13).

keyFigures.name: Moses and Pharaoh
keyFigures.role: Cited from Exodus to show God's mercy on whom he will have mercy and his hardening of Pharaoh (9:15-18).

keyFigures.name: Gentiles
keyFigures.role: Called as God's people according to Hosea, and attain righteousness by faith while Israel stumbles at the stumblingstone (9:24-26,30-33).

keyThemes.explanation: Paul has great heaviness for his kinsmen, to whom belong the adoption, the glory, the covenants, the law, and the promises (9:1-5).
God's word has not failed, for the promise follows his call through Isaac and Jacob, and he has mercy on whom he will have mercy (9:6-24).
Hosea and Isaiah show God calling a people from the Gentiles and saving a remnant of Israel, who stumbled at the stumblingstone (9:25-33).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the promise that Abraham's seed would be named through Isaac.
Paul quotes the promise that Sarah would have a son.
Paul quotes the statement about Jacob and Esau.
Paul quotes God's words about having mercy and compassion.
Paul quotes God's statement to Pharaoh about displaying divine power.
Paul quotes God's words about calling those formerly not his people his people.
Paul quotes Hosea's declaration that those not called God's people will be called his sons.
Paul explicitly quotes Isaiah's statement that only a remnant of Israel will be saved.
Paul quotes Isaiah's warning that without a surviving remnant Israel would resemble Sodom.

Romans 10.summary: Paul expresses his heartfelt desire and prayer for Israel's salvation (Romans 10:1). He criticizes zeal lacking knowledge of God's righteousness and explains that Christ is the goal or culmination of the Law for righteousness to everyone who believes (Romans 10:2–4). Contrasting scriptural descriptions of righteousness, he portrays the word of faith as near, connected to confessing Jesus as Lord and believing God raised him from the dead (Romans 10:5–13). Paul's quotations stress that everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved; he then traces the sequence from sending and preaching to hearing and faith (Romans 10:14–17). He closes by asking whether Israel has heard and understood, quoting Moses and Isaiah about God's outreach and Israel's resistance (Romans 10:18–21). The chapter holds together Paul's universal gospel invitation, concern for Israel, and the need for proclamation.
Romans 10.whereWeAre: Chapter 9 ended with Israel stumbling at the stone laid in Zion (9:32-33). Chapter 10 shows Paul praying for his people's salvation, explaining that Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, and tracing how faith comes through sending, preaching, and hearing (10:1-21). Chapter 11 asks whether Israel's stumbling is final.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Prays for Israel's salvation, saying they have a zeal of God but not according to knowledge (10:1-3).

keyFigures.name: Israel
keyFigures.role: Pursues righteousness by the law and stumbles, yet is told that God has stretched out his hands all day long to a disobedient people (10:3,21).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: The end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, confessed as Lord and believed raised from the dead (10:4,9).

keyFigures.name: Moses and Isaiah
keyFigures.role: Quoted to describe the word of faith near at hand and to show Gentiles finding God while Israel resists (10:5-8,16,19-21).

keyThemes.explanation: Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes, and confessing him as Lord and believing he was raised brings salvation (10:3-10).
There is no difference between Jew and Greek, for whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved (10:11-13).
Paul traces calling, believing, hearing, preaching, and sending, ending that faith cometh by hearing and hearing by the word of God (10:14-17).
Quoting Moses and Isaiah, Paul says Israel has heard yet remains a disobedient and gainsaying people toward whom God stretches out his hands (10:18-21).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the law's statement that the person who does these things will live by them.
Paul quotes Moses' question about ascending into heaven.
Paul directly quotes the statement that the word is near, in the mouth and heart.
Same event: These passages quote the declaration about trusting in the cornerstone in Zion.
Paul quotes the declaration that whoever calls on the Lord will be saved.
Paul quotes the announcement of good news brought by those with beautiful feet.
Paul quotes Isaiah's question about who believed the report.
Paul quotes the psalm's words about a message going out through all the earth.
Paul quotes God's declaration about provoking Israel through a people not considered a nation.
Paul quotes Isaiah about being found by those who did not seek him.
Paul quotes Isaiah about reaching out to a disobedient people.

Romans 11.summary: Paul emphatically denies that God has rejected his people, citing his own identity as an Israelite and Elijah's account of a faithful remnant (Romans 11:1–10). He argues that Israel's stumbling is not the end of the story: salvation has come to Gentiles, and this should not breed arrogance (Romans 11:11–15). In the olive-tree metaphor, Gentile believers are branches grafted into a cultivated tree and warned not to boast over broken-off branches (Romans 11:16–24). Paul speaks of a partial hardening until the fullness of Gentiles comes in, and declares that “all Israel shall be saved,” a phrase Christians have read in different ways (Romans 11:25–32). He ends with a doxology praising God's unsearchable wisdom (Romans 11:33–36).
Romans 11.whereWeAre: Chapter 10 ended with God stretching out his hands to a disobedient and contrary people (10:21). Chapter 11 answers that God has not cast them away: Paul points to himself and a remnant, pictures Gentile believers as wild branches grafted into Israel's olive tree, and praises the depth of God's wisdom (11:1-36). That doxology closes the argument and opens chapter 12's call to live it out.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Points to himself as an Israelite to show God has not cast away his people, and warns Gentile believers against boasting (11:1,13-24).

keyFigures.name: Elijah
keyFigures.role: Recalled for complaining that he alone was left, and for the answer that God had reserved seven thousand men (11:2-4).

keyFigures.name: Israel and Gentiles
keyFigures.role: Pictured as natural branches broken off and wild olive branches grafted in, with a promise that all Israel shall be saved (11:17-26).

keyFigures.name: God
keyFigures.role: Has not cast away his people, grafts branches in and can graft them in again, and is praised for the depth of his wisdom and knowledge (11:1-2,23,33-36).

keyThemes.explanation: God has not cast away his people; Paul is himself an Israelite, and a remnant exists according to the election of grace (11:1-6).
Gentile believers are wild branches grafted into the olive tree and are warned not to boast against the branches (11:17-24).
Blindness in part has happened to Israel until the fulness of the Gentiles comes in, and God has concluded all in unbelief that he might have mercy on all (11:25-32).
Paul ends in praise for the depth of the riches of God's wisdom and knowledge, for of him, and through him, and to him are all things (11:33-36).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes Elijah's complaint about killed prophets and demolished altars.
Paul quotes God's reply that seven thousand had not bowed to Baal.
Paul quotes the psalm's words about a table becoming a snare and eyes growing dark.
Paul quotes the question about who has known the mind of the Lord.

Romans 12.summary: Paul shifts from sustained theological argument to practical exhortation. He urges believers to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and be transformed by renewed minds rather than molded by the age (Romans 12:1–2). He calls for humble judgment about oneself and describes the church as one body with many members and different gifts (Romans 12:3–8). A series of instructions urges sincere love, mutual honor, hospitality, perseverance, prayer, empathy and peace (Romans 12:9–18). Rather than retaliate, believers are told to leave vengeance to God and overcome evil with good, even feeding a hungry enemy (Romans 12:19–21). The chapter shows how Paul's theology is meant to shape relationships.
Romans 12.whereWeAre: Chapter 11 ended with praise that all things are of God, through him, and to him (11:36). Chapter 12 turns from argument to life: Paul urges believers, in view of God's mercies, to present themselves as a living sacrifice, serve as one body with different gifts, love sincerely, and overcome evil with good (12:1-21). Chapter 13 extends that conduct to governing authorities and neighbors.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Beseeches believers by God's mercies to present their bodies as a living sacrifice and be transformed by the renewing of their minds (12:1-2).

keyFigures.name: Believers as one body
keyFigures.role: Many members in one body in Christ, each with a different gift to use for the others (12:4-8).

keyFigures.name: Enemies and persecutors
keyFigures.role: Those who curse or wrong believers, who are told to bless and not curse, and to overcome evil with good (12:14,17-21).

keyThemes.explanation: In view of God's mercies, believers present their bodies a living sacrifice and are transformed by the renewing of their minds (12:1-2).
Believers are many members in one body, each using a different gift for the others (12:3-8).
Paul urges love without dissimulation, kindness, hospitality, rejoicing with those who rejoice and weeping with those who weep (12:9-16).
Believers are told not to repay evil for evil but to feed a hungry enemy and overcome evil with good (12:17-21).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes God's declaration that vengeance and repayment belong to him.
Paul quotes the instruction to feed and give drink to an enemy.

Romans 13.summary: Paul tells believers to recognize governing authorities and explains authority in relation to public order and accountability (Romans 13:1–7). He urges payment of taxes and appropriate respect, although Christians have long asked how these instructions apply when rulers act unjustly. He then says that the continuing debt is to love one another, citing commandments against adultery, murder, theft and coveting, all summed up in love of neighbor (Romans 13:8–10). With the time of salvation nearer, Paul uses day-and-night imagery to urge rejection of destructive conduct and a life shaped by Christ (Romans 13:11–14). The chapter joins civic responsibility, neighbor-love and moral vigilance, not an unconditional endorsement of every state action.
Romans 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 ended with the call to overcome evil with good (12:21). Chapter 13 applies it publicly: believers are to be subject to governing authorities and pay what they owe, to owe no one anything but love, and to wake from sleep because salvation is nearer than when they believed (13:1-14). Chapter 14 brings the same love to disagreements inside the church.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Tells believers to be subject to the higher powers, to pay what is owed, and to owe no one anything but love (13:1-8).

keyFigures.name: Governing authorities
keyFigures.role: Described as God's ministers who bear the sword, praise good conduct, and punish evil (13:1-4).

keyFigures.name: Neighbors and fellow believers
keyFigures.role: The ones believers are told to love, since love is the fulfilling of the law (13:8-10).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: The Lord whom believers are told to put on, making no provision for the flesh (13:14).

keyThemes.explanation: Believers are to be subject to the higher powers as God's ministers, and to render tribute, custom, fear, and honor to whom each is due (13:1-7).
Owing no one anything but to love one another, believers fulfil the law, since love works no ill to his neighbour (13:8-10).
Because salvation is nearer, believers are to cast off the works of darkness and put on the Lord Jesus Christ (13:11-14).

explainedReferences.explanation: The command against murder is explicitly repeated.
The command against adultery is explicitly repeated.
The command against stealing is explicitly repeated.
Paul quotes the command to love your neighbor as yourself.

Romans 14.summary: Paul instructs believers to welcome those whose convictions about food differ, rather than quarrel over disputable matters (Romans 14:1–4). Some observe particular days while others regard every day alike; each should act with conviction before the Lord (Romans 14:5–9). Because all will answer to God, believers should not despise or judge one another (Romans 14:10–12). Freedom should not become a cause of stumbling for another: the kingdom of God is characterized by righteousness, peace and joy in the Holy Spirit rather than food and drink (Romans 14:13–18). Paul urges mutual peace and building up the community, and warns against violating one's conscience (Romans 14:19–23).
Romans 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 ended with Paul telling believers to put on the Lord Jesus Christ (13:14). Chapter 14 shows what that means among believers who disagree about food and holy days: welcome one another, stop judging, answer to the Lord, and do not cause a brother to stumble, since the kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost (14:1-23). Chapter 15 carries that unity into Paul's plans.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Calls believers to welcome one another without quarreling over doubtful things such as food and days (14:1-6).

keyFigures.name: The weak in faith
keyFigures.role: Believers who eat only herbs or esteem one day above another, and are told not to be judged or despised (14:1-6).

keyFigures.name: Those who eat all things
keyFigures.role: Believers with broader freedom, told not to despise the weak or put a stumblingblock in a brother's way (14:3,13-21).

keyFigures.name: The Lord
keyFigures.role: The master before whom each believer stands or falls, and before whose judgment seat all will give account (14:4,10-12).

keyThemes.explanation: Believers are to receive the one who is weak in faith without quarreling over doubtful things such as food and days (14:1-6).
Whether living or dying, believers are the Lord's, and each will give account of himself to God at the judgment seat of Christ (14:7-12).
The kingdom of God is righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost, so believers avoid putting a stumblingblock before a brother (14:13-23).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes God's declaration that every knee will bow and tongue confess.

Romans 15.summary: Paul continues the theme of mutual care: the strong should bear with the weak, following Christ's example of self-giving rather than self-pleasing (Romans 15:1–6). He commands mutual welcome and argues from Scripture that Jesus' ministry confirms God's promises to Israel while Gentiles also praise God (Romans 15:7–13). Paul then speaks personally of his ministry among Gentiles, his desire to preach where Christ is not yet named, and his travel plan: take a collection for impoverished believers in Jerusalem, visit Rome and continue toward Spain (Romans 15:14–29). He requests prayer for protection and a welcomeable outcome in Jerusalem (Romans 15:30–33). The chapter joins communal unity and practical mission planning.
Romans 15.whereWeAre: Chapter 14 ended with Paul warning against acting against conscience (14:23). Chapter 15 asks the strong to bear with the weak as Christ did, urges Jews and Gentiles to glorify God together, and shares Paul's plans to carry a collection to Jerusalem and then visit Rome on the way to Spain (15:1-33). Chapter 16 fills in the people behind those plans.

keyFigures.name: Paul
keyFigures.role: Describes his ministry to the Gentiles, his plan to bring a collection to Jerusalem, and his hope to visit Rome on the way to Spain (15:14-29).

keyFigures.name: Jesus Christ
keyFigures.role: Pleased not himself and became a minister of the circumcision to confirm the promises, so that Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy (15:3,8-9).

keyFigures.name: Gentile believers
keyFigures.role: Share in the collection for the poor saints at Jerusalem, having been made partakers of their spiritual things (15:26-27).

keyFigures.name: Poor believers in Jerusalem
keyFigures.role: The recipients of a gift from Macedonia and Achaia that Paul carries to them (15:25-26).

keyThemes.explanation: The strong bear the infirmities of the weak, receiving one another as Christ received them to the glory of God (15:1-7).
Christ confirmed the promises to the fathers so that Gentiles might also glorify God for his mercy, as the Scriptures foretold (15:8-13).
Paul describes preaching where Christ was not named, and his plan to carry the Macedonian and Achaian gift to Jerusalem before going to Spain (15:14-29).
Paul asks the Romans to strive with him in prayer that he may be delivered from unbelievers in Judea and that his service be accepted (15:30-33).

explainedReferences.explanation: Paul quotes the psalm about reproaches falling on the speaker.
Paul quotes the psalm's declaration of praise among the Gentiles.
Paul quotes the call for the nations to rejoice with God's people.
Paul quotes the command for all nations and peoples to praise the Lord.
Paul quotes Isaiah about the root of Jesse and hope for the nations.
Paul quotes the promise that those not told will see and understand.

Romans 16.summary: Paul commends Phebe, described as a servant or deacon of the church at Cenchrea and a benefactor of many, asking the Romans to receive and help her (Romans 16:1–2). He greets Priscilla and Aquila, the church in their house, and numerous other believers, women and men, acknowledging their labor and relationships (Romans 16:3–16). He warns against people who create division through teaching contrary to what the community learned (Romans 16:17–20). Greetings follow from companions, including Timothy and Tertius, who identifies himself as the one who wrote the letter down (Romans 16:21–23). The book closes with praise to God for the revealed gospel (Romans 16:25–27); the placement of this doxology varies in ancient manuscript traditions. The chapter vividly illustrates a geographically dispersed, collaborative network of early Christian communities.
Romans 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 ended with Paul asking for prayer for his journey to Jerusalem (15:30-33). Chapter 16 commends Phebe, who probably carried the letter, greets many named believers, warns against those who cause divisions, and closes with greetings and a doxology (16:1-27). That personal network leads into the letters Paul wrote to the churches he had already planted, beginning with 1 Corinthians.

keyFigures.name: Phebe
keyFigures.role: A servant of the church at Cenchrea and a succourer of many, commended to the Romans and probably the letter's carrier (16:1-2).

keyFigures.name: Priscilla and Aquila
keyFigures.role: Paul's helpers in Christ Jesus who risked their necks for his life and host a church in their house (16:3-5).

keyFigures.name: Andronicus and Junia
keyFigures.role: Paul's kinsmen and fellow prisoners, described as of note among the apostles and in Christ before Paul (16:7).

keyFigures.name: Timothy and Tertius
keyFigures.role: Timothy sends greetings, and Tertius identifies himself as the one who wrote the letter (16:21-22).

keyFigures.name: Other greeted believers
keyFigures.role: Many named men, women, and households whom Paul greets and honors for their labor in the Lord (16:5-16).

keyThemes.explanation: Paul commends Phebe and greets Priscilla, Aquila, Andronicus, and Junia as fellow workers and fellow prisoners in Christ (16:1-7).
Paul greets a church in Priscilla and Aquila's house and many named believers, women and men, for their labor in the Lord (16:3-16).
Paul urges believers to mark those who cause divisions contrary to the doctrine they learned, and promises that God will bruise Satan under their feet (16:17-20).
The letter ends in glory to God, who is able to establish believers according to the gospel and the revelation of the mystery now made known to all nations (16:25-27).
